text: Mohammed Racim (Arabic: محمد راسم, 24 June 1896 – 30 March 1975) was an Algerian artist who co-founded the Algerian School for Miniature Painting with his brother, Omar, and the institution continues to exist today.[1] Born in the Casbah of Algiers in 1896 into a distinguished family of artists,[1][2] Racim came from a lineage whose pre-colonial prosperity was diminished by the French regime's confiscation of property.[1][3] In 1880, his father had re-established a wood-carving and copper-working workshop in the Casbah, where Omar Racim engraved decorative tombstones. The family secured commissions to decorate public buildings and pavilions at French colonial exhibitions.[4] Racim's talent for drawing was recognized during his primary education when he was assigned to copy Islamic decorative motifs for state workshops established by Governor Charles Jonnart. Around 1914, he became familiar with Persian, Mughal, and Andalusian miniatures created for the private use of Muslim nobility and developed a personal style blending traditional materials and classical arabesque and calligraphic elements with figurative inserts that included modern features. As a teenager, he befriended Nasreddine Dinet, who advised him on painting the human figure and helped him secure commissions to decorate books with calligraphic plates. His primary patrons were businessmen and government officials who appreciated his depictions of old Algeria's cultural milieu.[1] By the late 1930s, Racim had become a prominent figure in Algerian culture.[3] His work "Women at the Cascade" presents an imagined pre-colonial past, depicting a time before French arrival when indigenous people were masters of the Maghreb, portrayed as prosperous, engaged in fine textiles, elaborate costumes, and the arts of music, architecture, and gardening.[5] Roger Benjamin has argued that Racim's work effectively erases the presence of French settlers in Algeria, celebrating a pristine Turkish city rather than the industrialized port shaped by a century of French modernization. Nevertheless, he was not an ideologue and acknowledged that his artistic success was made possible by French scholarly influence.[6] Mohammed Racim and his wife were killed in their home on 30 March 1975 and were buried together in the Thaalibia Cemetery of the Casbah of Algiers.[citation needed] On 24 June 2021, Google honored his 125th birthday with a Google Doodle.[7]
